newsitem.title: SPAIN: Mexico keen to free up more Brady bond collateral.
newsitem.headline: Mexico keen to free up more Brady bond collateral.

text.p: Mexico said on Monday it was unlikely to repeat the exchange it carried out last year to retire its Brady debt but was still seeking ways of freeing the collateral tied up in its Brady bonds.
In a landmark move in May 1996, Mexico retired some of its outstanding Brady bonds by auctioning Par and Discount instruments for a $1.75 billion 30-year global bond.
Although a resounding success, the transaction exposed the Mexican market to about two weeks of volatility while the procedure was being carried out.

"Having done that, we don't think we need to use the same structure in future," Mexico's Deputy Finance Minister Martin Werner told reporters ahead of the opening of the Inter-American Development Bank's 38th annual meeting.

"The option is a very complicated procedure and there is uncertainty linked to a particular week or two weeks of the option process. We are thankful we did it once but we don't think we in the future it's probably the best structure," he added.

So-called Brady bonds were created after the debt crisis of the early 1980s when many Latin American countries defaulted on their commercial obligations. The debt was restructured and particular instruments collateralised with zero coupon U.S. Treasuries.
Werner said Mexico was still interested in freeing up billions of dollars of collateral tied up in its outstanding Brady bonds.

"We still feel that the Bradys are inefficient instruments," he said. "Mexico still has today close to $7 billion invested in Brady collateral. If there are ways we can get our hands on that collateral...we will continue to (try to) do that."
He did not rule out further buybacks in future.

"As we have always said we are always looking at the market and if there are opportunities we will take advantage of that arbitrage to do it in the future," Werner said. --Caroline Brothers, Barcelona Newsroom + 34 3 242 2659
